scope: Chapter 1 Trade and Livelihood teaching and lesson order only; preserve images, assessments, trade configuration and rewards

expected.title: Daily Livelihood
expected.content: As you explore the community, you see people working to provide food and other needs for their families. Farming, fishing, and making useful goods are important parts of everyday life.
expected.exploreIntroduction: Look around the barangay! Different people are working to provide food and useful goods for their community. Explore each activity to discover how early Filipinos made a living.

exploreItems.title: The Farming Area
exploreItems.hint: Explore how people grew food.
exploreItems.discovery: In many early Filipino communities, people cultivated crops such as rice and root crops. Farming provided food and was shaped by local land, water, and environmental conditions.

exploreItems.title: The Fishing Area
exploreItems.hint: Discover how people gathered food from the water.
exploreItems.discovery: Communities near rivers, lakes, and seas could depend on fishing and other aquatic resources. People used knowledge of their environment and different fishing methods to help provide food.

exploreItems.title: The Crafting Area
exploreItems.hint: See how people made useful objects.
exploreItems.discovery: Skilled community members created useful products from available materials, including pottery, woven goods, and tools. These products supported daily activities and could also be exchanged through trade.

expected.discoveryTitle: How Early Filipinos Made a Living
expected.discoveryText: Early Filipino communities relied on different livelihood activities to meet their needs. Farming, fishing, and crafting helped provide food, tools, and useful goods. The activities of each community depended partly on its environment, available resources, and the skills of its people.
expected.keyTermDefinition: Livelihood refers to the work and activities people do to provide for their needs and support their families. In early Filipino communities, livelihoods included farming, fishing, making crafts, and trading goods.
expected.historicalInsight: Early Filipino communities depended on different livelihood activities such as farming, fishing, and crafts.

fields.title: Daily Livelihood: From Land to Food
fields.content:
In the previous mission, you investigated how people organized community life. Now follow a new problem: how can families obtain food and useful goods when no one can make everything alone? We will connect resources, skills, products and exchange.

A livelihood is work that helps people meet their needs. Farming, fishing and craft work could contribute in different ways. Suitable land or nearby water offers opportunities, but people also need knowledge, tools and cooperation. Not everyone in one place has the same job.

Worked example: a family has suitable soil and water. Step 1. Prepare the growing area and plant crops. Step 2. Care for the plants using farming knowledge. Step 3. Gather the harvest and plan how much the family needs. This connects a resource with work and a product: land and water, farming skills, then food. Crops and methods differed among communities; the example is not a record of one named historical village.
fields.exploreIntroduction: Open the three clues. Connect a resource, a skill, a product and a need.

exploreItems.title: Land and water
exploreItems.hint: Find an observation that helps explain the plan.
exploreItems.discovery: The fictional family has a suitable growing area and access to water. These resources make a farming plan possible, but do not do the work themselves.

exploreItems.title: Knowledge and work
exploreItems.hint: Find an observation that helps explain the plan.
exploreItems.discovery: Preparing soil, planting and caring for crops are learned activities. The process takes time rather than producing food as soon as a seed is planted.

exploreItems.title: Household needs first
exploreItems.hint: Find an observation that helps explain the plan.
exploreItems.discovery: A harvest provides food. Before offering products in exchange, a family should consider what it still needs for its own use.

fields.decisionSituation: A family has suitable growing land, water and farming knowledge. Which explanation connects these clues?
fields.decisionQuestion: Which explanation uses the lesson clues?
decisionChoices: People use resources and skills to grow food
The land provides a finished meal without work
Every person nearby must have the same livelihood
Growing crops means no other products can be useful
fields.decisionCorrectAnswer: People use resources and skills to grow food
fields.decisionExplanation: The example connects land and water with learned farming activities and a food harvest. Resources and human work contribute together.
fields.discoveryText: The example connects land and water with learned farming activities and a food harvest. Resources and human work contribute together.

expected.title: Goods from the Community
expected.content: You notice community members producing and gathering different goods. Some grow crops, others catch fish, while skilled workers create useful items from materials available around them.
expected.exploreIntroduction: You arrive at an area where community members are gathering food and working with the land and water around them. Explore the different environments to discover how natural resources influenced the livelihoods of early Filipinos.

exploreItems.title: The Farmland
exploreItems.hint: Explore how people used the land to grow food.
exploreItems.discovery: In communities with suitable land and water, early Filipinos cultivated crops such as rice and root crops. Farming methods varied according to the local environment and available resources.

exploreItems.title: Rivers and Coastal Waters
exploreItems.hint: Discover how nearby waters provided food.
exploreItems.discovery: Communities near rivers, lakes, and coastal waters could obtain fish and other aquatic resources. People developed fishing methods suited to their surroundings and used their knowledge of local waters.

exploreItems.title: Natural Materials
exploreItems.hint: Investigate how people used nearby materials.
exploreItems.discovery: Early Filipinos used locally available materials such as bamboo, wood, clay, and plant fibers to create useful objects. The materials found in an area influenced the products people could make.

expected.discoveryText: The environment influenced how early Filipino communities made a living. People in areas with suitable farmland could grow crops, while communities near rivers and seas could obtain food through fishing. Natural materials such as bamboo, wood, clay, and plant fibers also helped people create useful products. Livelihood activities varied depending on local resources, skills, and surroundings.
expected.historicalInsight: The natural resources available to communities influenced the kinds of livelihood activities people practiced.

fields.title: Fishing: Resources Need Knowledge
fields.content:
Next, follow fishers preparing to work near coastal waters. Fish are a resource, but a successful livelihood also depends on knowledge, equipment and conditions. People learn where and how to work through experience and teaching.

Connect the stages. First, people prepare suitable gear and use knowledge of the water. Next, a catch can provide food. Families then prepare the fish for meals and decide how to use what is available. Fishing is a livelihood because the work helps meet a need, not simply because the community lives beside water.

Compare this with farming. Both use environmental resources and human skill to produce food, but the resources and methods differ. A coastal place can also have farmers, makers and other workers. Some products may be exchanged after household needs are considered. The scene is a fictional learning example; it does not describe one method used everywhere in the past.
fields.exploreIntroduction: Open the three clues. Connect a resource, a skill, a product and a need.

exploreItems.title: Food from water
exploreItems.hint: Find an observation that helps explain the plan.
exploreItems.discovery: A catch can help provide meals. Fish and other aquatic resources contribute differently from crops grown on land.

exploreItems.title: Preparation matters
exploreItems.hint: Find an observation that helps explain the plan.
exploreItems.discovery: Gear must suit the activity and people need knowledge of local water conditions. Having a shoreline alone does not supply a ready catch.

exploreItems.title: Compare two livelihoods
exploreItems.hint: Find an observation that helps explain the plan.
exploreItems.discovery: Farming and fishing both connect work with food needs. Their tools and resources differ, so one example should not stand for every community.

fields.decisionSituation: A learner says living beside the sea is all that is needed for fishing. Which information improves the explanation?
fields.decisionQuestion: Which explanation uses the lesson clues?
decisionChoices: The shoreline means every person must fish
The name of a place tells us its exact catch
Fishing means crops and crafts cannot be useful
People also need suitable skills, equipment and knowledge of conditions
fields.decisionCorrectAnswer: People also need suitable skills, equipment and knowledge of conditions
fields.decisionExplanation: Water offers resources, while people contribute knowledge and equipment. Location creates opportunities rather than assigning everyone one job.
fields.discoveryText: Water offers resources, while people contribute knowledge and equipment. Location creates opportunities rather than assigning everyone one job.

expected.title: Trading with Others
expected.content: Near the shore, you see people exchanging goods with visitors from other communities. Products they have in abundance can be traded for things that are harder to obtain locally.
expected.exploreIntroduction: You arrive at a busy trading place near the shore. People from different communities are exchanging useful goods. Explore what they brought and discover why trade was important to early Filipino communities.

exploreItems.title: Goods from the Community
exploreItems.hint: Discover what people brought to exchange.
exploreItems.discovery: Early Filipino communities could exchange products such as crops, woven goods, pottery, and other locally made items. The goods available for trade depended on the resources and skills of each community.

exploreItems.title: Visiting Traders
exploreItems.hint: Find out why people traveled to exchange goods.
exploreItems.discovery: People traveled between communities to exchange products. Trade also connected some early Filipino communities with merchants from other parts of Asia, allowing goods, ideas, and cultural influences to move between places.

exploreItems.title: Exchanging Useful Goods
exploreItems.hint: Investigate why communities traded.
exploreItems.discovery: Not every community produced the same goods. Through trade, people could obtain useful products that were less available in their own area. Exchanges depended on the needs, resources, and relationships of the people involved.

expected.discoveryText: Early Filipino communities exchanged goods to obtain products they needed or valued. They traded locally produced items such as crops, pottery, and woven goods. Trade connected different communities and, in some areas, brought people into contact with merchants from other parts of Asia. These exchanges helped support livelihoods and encouraged the sharing of goods, knowledge, and ideas.
expected.historicalInsight: Trade allowed early Filipino communities to exchange products and obtain resources from other places.

fields.title: Trade: Check Both Communities Needs
fields.content:
Imagine two communities in a made-up teaching example. One has fish available for exchange but needs containers. Another makes suitable containers but needs food. Trading could connect the different products and needs.

Work through a plan. Step 1. Ask what each group can offer after keeping what it needs. Step 2. Ask what each wants to receive. Step 3. Discuss an exchange both accept. A list of available products is not enough; the plan must address the two groups' needs.

Barter is a direct exchange of goods or services without money. A fisher exchanging some fish for a basket is a barter example. Trade is the wider idea of exchange, and can help people obtain products or materials not easily available nearby. The example does not mean all early exchanges had one fixed price or that every community stopped making its own goods.
fields.exploreIntroduction: Open the three clues. Connect a resource, a skill, a product and a need.

exploreItems.title: Offer and need differ
exploreItems.hint: Find an observation that helps explain the plan.
exploreItems.discovery: Fish are what one group can offer; a container is what it needs. Mixing these up can produce a plan that helps neither side.

exploreItems.title: Check the partner
exploreItems.hint: Find an observation that helps explain the plan.
exploreItems.discovery: The makers need food and can offer containers. The needs of both sides matter when considering a useful exchange.

exploreItems.title: Agree rather than assume
exploreItems.hint: Find an observation that helps explain the plan.
exploreItems.discovery: A quantity in a teaching exchange is an agreement for that activity. It is not a price established for all early Philippine communities.

fields.decisionSituation: Fishers need containers and container makers need food. Which plan connects both needs?
fields.decisionQuestion: Which explanation uses the lesson clues?
decisionChoices: Choose quantities without checking available supplies
Assume trade means both groups stop producing their own goods
Discuss exchanging some fish for suitable containers
Give the makers more containers without checking their needs
fields.decisionCorrectAnswer: Discuss exchanging some fish for suitable containers
fields.decisionExplanation: Trade can connect different supplies and needs. A useful plan checks both groups, available quantities and an accepted agreement.
fields.discoveryText: Trade can connect different supplies and needs. A useful plan checks both groups, available quantities and an accepted agreement.
fields.keyTermDefinition: Directly exchanging goods or services without money.
fields.historicalInsight: This scene is a fictional teaching example. Resources, skills and arrangements varied among early communities; living traditions are not proof of identical past practices.

learningHelp.explanation: Trade can connect different supplies and needs. A useful plan checks both groups, available quantities and an accepted agreement.

expected.title: Skills and Crafts
expected.content:
As you continue exploring the community, you hear the sounds of people working with different materials. Nearby, someone shapes clay into a pot, while others weave plant fibers into useful containers and prepare tools for daily activities.
You discover that making these objects requires knowledge, practice, and skill. People use materials available in their surroundings to create products that help their families and communities.
Some of these useful goods can also be exchanged with other communities.
expected.exploreIntroduction: You enter a busy crafting area where skilled community members are making useful objects. Explore three activities to discover how early Filipinos transformed natural materials into everyday products.

exploreItems.title: Making Clay Pots
exploreItems.hint: Discover how clay became useful containers.
exploreItems.discovery: Early Filipino potters shaped clay into containers used for cooking, storing food, and other daily activities. Pottery required knowledge of materials, shaping techniques, and firing.

exploreItems.title: Weaving Plant Fibers
exploreItems.hint: Explore how plants became useful woven goods.
exploreItems.discovery: People in different communities used plant fibers and other suitable materials to weave baskets, mats, and other useful products. Weaving required skill and knowledge passed through generations.

exploreItems.title: Making Useful Tools
exploreItems.hint: Investigate how materials became everyday tools.
exploreItems.discovery: Early Filipinos made tools using materials such as wood, stone, and metal, depending on local resources and available technology. These tools supported activities including farming, fishing, and other work.

expected.decisionSituation: A family in an early Filipino community needs a container to store harvested grains. A skilled craftsperson has access to clay, bamboo, and plant fibers. The family asks for a sturdy container that can help protect their stored food.
expected.decisionQuestion: Which choice best shows how craftsmanship can help the family meet its needs? Copy
decisionChoices: Shape and fire clay into a suitable storage pot.
Leave the grains on the ground without a container.
Stop making useful objects because natural materials cannot be used.
Throw away the available materials instead of using them.
expected.decisionCorrectAnswer: Shape and fire clay into a suitable storage pot.
expected.decisionExplanation: Early Filipino craftspeople used their knowledge and skills to turn natural materials into useful products. A properly made clay pot could help a family store harvested food. This shows how craftsmanship supported everyday needs and livelihoods.
expected.discoveryTitle: How Craft Skills Supported Daily Life
expected.discoveryText: Early Filipino communities developed skills to turn natural materials into useful products. Pottery provided containers for cooking and storage, weaving produced baskets and mats, and toolmaking supported work such as farming and fishing. These crafts helped meet everyday needs, and some finished products could also be exchanged through trade.
expected.keyTermDefinition: Craftsmanship is the skill of making useful or decorative objects by hand. In early Filipino communities, skilled people made pottery, woven goods, tools, and other products using materials available in their surroundings.
expected.historicalInsight: Early Filipino communities developed different craft skills, including pottery, weaving, and toolmaking. These skills helped people transform natural materials into useful products. Craft traditions and available materials varied across communities.

fields.title: Craft Skills: From Materials to a Product
fields.content:
Before planning the final exchange, visit a workshop. A family needs a suitable pot for storing grain. Clay by itself is not a finished storage container: a maker needs knowledge of preparing, shaping and firing it.

Follow a worked material-to-product example. Step 1. Choose suitable clay and understand its properties. Step 2. Shape the container using learned skills. Step 3. Fire and finish it using appropriate techniques. The result can support a household need or become a product for exchange. This describes skilled work, not instructions for children to fire pottery.

Weaving also turns materials into useful products. Makers select and prepare suitable plant materials, then use skill to form baskets or mats. Different products suit different purposes. Museum examples help explain materials and knowledge; present-day traditions are not proof that every precolonial community worked in exactly the same way.
fields.exploreIntroduction: Open the three clues. Connect a resource, a skill, a product and a need.

exploreItems.title: Match purpose and material
exploreItems.hint: Find an observation that helps explain the plan.
exploreItems.discovery: A storage container must suit the material being stored. Choosing an attractive material without considering the task is not enough.

exploreItems.title: Notice the learned process
exploreItems.hint: Find an observation that helps explain the plan.
exploreItems.discovery: Preparing, shaping and firing clay require knowledge. A finished pot reflects skilled work as well as raw material.

exploreItems.title: Compare another craft
exploreItems.hint: Find an observation that helps explain the plan.
exploreItems.discovery: Baskets and mats require prepared materials and weaving knowledge. Calling them simple objects can hide the skill used to make them.

fields.decisionSituation: A family needs a suitable grain-storage pot and a maker has clay and pottery skills. Which plan fits?
fields.decisionQuestion: Which explanation uses the lesson clues?
decisionChoices: Assume a new material removes the need for any skill
Prepare, shape and fire a suitable container using learned techniques
Treat unshaped clay as a finished storage container
Choose a product without considering what it will hold
fields.decisionCorrectAnswer: Prepare, shape and fire a suitable container using learned techniques
fields.decisionExplanation: Craftsmanship connects a purpose, appropriate materials and learned techniques. Clay becomes a useful pot through skilled work, not by its availability alone.
fields.discoveryText: Craftsmanship connects a purpose, appropriate materials and learned techniques. Clay becomes a useful pot through skilled work, not by its availability alone.
fields.keyTermDefinition: Skill and knowledge used to make useful or decorative objects.

expected.title: The Livelihood Challenge
expected.content:
Before leaving the community, you meet several families preparing for their daily activities. Some are gathering food, others are making useful objects, and a group of traders is preparing to exchange goods with a nearby community.
A community elder invites you to think about what you have discovered. How can people use their surroundings, skills, and available products to meet different needs?
You prepare to apply what you have learned about farming, fishing, natural resources, crafts, and trade.
expected.historicalInsight: Early Filipino communities used their knowledge of the environment, natural resources, and practical skills to support their livelihoods. Farming, fishing, crafts, and trade helped people meet everyday needs. These activities varied according to each community's location and resources.

fields.title: Field Journal: Explain the Exchange
fields.content:
You have now completed the exchange investigation. Connect what made a working plan possible, instead of remembering quantities alone. The grain came from farming work; the pots required materials and craft knowledge. The agreement and available supplies shaped what each group could exchange.

Build your explanation with four links: resources, skills, products and needs. A resource provides an opportunity. People apply knowledge and work to make or gather a product. Households keep what they need, and exchange may help obtain other useful products. Different people and communities can contribute different activities.

Review your plan: what did each side offer, what did each receive, and why did that help? The activity agreement was fictional, not a price for every past community. Saving a clue in your Evidence Journal preserves a learning reference, not ownership of real goods. Next, the chapter challenge asks you to apply what you learned about community life and livelihoods.
fields.exploreIntroduction: Open the three clues. Connect a resource, a skill, a product and a need.

exploreItems.title: Trace the grain
exploreItems.hint: Find an observation that helps explain the plan.
exploreItems.discovery: In the teaching example, grain represents food produced through farming. It is not an unlimited supply that can be spent without considering needs.

exploreItems.title: Trace the pots
exploreItems.hint: Find an observation that helps explain the plan.
exploreItems.discovery: Pots represent material preparation and craft knowledge. Exchange connects that work with people who need containers.

exploreItems.title: Explain the benefit
exploreItems.hint: Find an observation that helps explain the plan.
exploreItems.discovery: A valid exchange checks goods, quantities, both needs and the activity agreement. Following a number alone does not explain why the plan helps.

expected.introduction:
Travel back to the Philippines before Spanish colonization and discover how early Filipino communities made a living.
Explore farms, fishing areas, workshops, and trading places. Investigate how people used natural resources, developed useful skills, and exchanged goods to support their families and communities.
Follow historical clues, make thoughtful decisions, and prepare for your Mission Trial.
expected.learningObjective: Explain how farming, fishing, crafts, natural resources, and trade supported the livelihood and economic activities of early Filipino communities.
learningObjectives: Connect farming and fishing to local environments and food needs.
Explain how craft skills produced useful objects.
Describe how exchanging products could meet different community needs.
expected.lessonRecap: Farming, fishing and craft skills helped communities use local resources for daily needs. Trade connected communities with different products and resources.

fields.introduction: Connect resources, skills, products and needs. Follow farming, fishing and craft examples, plan an exchange, then explain how it helps both groups.
fields.learningObjective: Explain how resources and skilled work support livelihoods, then apply supplies, needs and an agreement to a fictional exchange.
learningObjectives: Connect farming resources and learned activities with food production.
Explain why fishing needs knowledge and equipment as well as nearby water.
Connect suitable materials and craft skills with useful products.
Check both communities supplies and needs before proposing barter.
Explain how exchange can provide products not easily available locally.
fields.lessonRecap: Farming, fishing and craft work connect resources and skills with food and useful products. Communities can have different resources and needs. A useful exchange considers both sides, available quantities and an agreement. The activity quantities are fictional teaching values, not historical prices for every community.
